title: Sugar Stocks Soar Up to 59% on Dalal Street, but Analysts Warn Valuations Are Running Ahead
excerpt: Rising domestic prices, tight global supplies and El Niño fears have sent sugar counters surging, yet experts say the market has already priced in two strong quarters.
body:
• Sugar stocks rallied up to 59% in August, led by Avadh Sugar & Energy, as domestic prices hit record levels amid supply concerns and a global deficit estimated at 3.3 million tonnes.
  • The government has tightened stockholding limits for bulk consumers and banned sugar exports through September 2026, signalling it will intervene against price inflation.
  • Analysts are divided: some see a fundamental re-rating as mills pivot to ethanol and biofuel, while others warn the rally has pre-paid for peak-season earnings that may not last.
  • DAM Capital estimates opening inventory for the 2026-27 season at just 3 million tonnes — enough for only 35 days of consumption and the lowest in a decade.

A Record-Setting August for Sugar Counters

Indian sugar stocks emerged as one of the strongest pockets of the market in August, with several counters delivering explosive gains as domestic prices climbed to record levels. Avadh Sugar & Energy led the pack with a 59.35% gain, closing at ₹804.15 compared with ₹504.65 on July 31, according to data compiled by The Economic Times.

Dwarikesh Sugar Industries rose 38%, Dalmia Bharat Sugar gained 35.63%, and Uttam Sugar Mills and Mawana Sugars advanced 33.66% and 32.52% respectively. Among larger companies, Balrampur Chini Mills gained 10.63%, while Shree Renuka Sugars rose 7.19%. Godavari Biorefineries was the lone decliner, falling 8.51%.

The all-India average ex-mill sugar price rose to around ₹5,400–5,500 per quintal from about ₹3,900 a year earlier. Average retail prices reached ₹52.30 per kilogram on August 18, up roughly 13% year-on-year, according to Outlook Business.

"The market has effectively pre-paid for two strong quarters."

— Harshal Dasani, Business Head, INVasset PMS

What Is Driving the Rally

The immediate trigger has been a sharp rise in sugar prices, improving expectations around mill realisations and profitability. A combination of factors has tightened supply: lower-than-expected production, steady domestic consumption, and diversion of cane towards ethanol have resulted in declining inventories.

Concerns over crop conditions in Maharashtra and Karnataka have deepened worries about the coming season, while adverse weather in top global producers like Brazil and Thailand has tightened international supply. The government estimated a global sugar deficit of around 3.3 million tonnes for 2026-27, according to official statements. International prices rose from $474 per tonne on June 30 to $552 per tonne by August 20 — a 16% jump in less than two months.

DAM Capital Advisors estimates sugar inventory at the start of the 2026-27 season on October 1 at around 3 million tonnes, enough for only 35 days of consumption and the lowest opening stock in a decade. "Deficit rainfall threatens SS27 cane yields, and an advanced start to the crush will compress recovery, leaving the system in sustained deficit for at least the next fifteen months," the brokerage said.

The Ethanol Re-Rating Thesis

Avinash Gorakshakar, founder of Avinash Mentor Research, said the rally reflects a fundamental re-rating of the sector. "The market is no longer treating these companies purely as cyclical agricultural businesses — they are increasingly being valued as structural green energy and biofuel plays," he said.

India's push toward the 1,000-plus crore litre ethanol requirement for the 2025-26 cycle has underpinned this narrative. Faster-than-expected procurement by oil marketing companies would lock in revenue visibility for sugar companies, Gorakshakar noted. However, he cautioned that with the sugarcane Fair and Remunerative Price having risen 16%, ethanol procurement prices — especially from B-heavy molasses — have lagged.

Why Valuations May Be Stretched

Despite the improving fundamentals, several analysts argue the rally has already discounted the near-term earnings improvement. Harshal Dasani of INVasset PMS pointed out that a 60% stock move is discounting the full benefit of retail prices up 25% in a month, but "mill economics capture that surge only partially and with a lag, since domestic sales flow through the government's monthly release mechanism and the crushing season's real earnings arrive only from the October-November crush."

Dasani also warned that sugar is a policy-managed commodity in both directions. "The very stockholding order that lit this rally is the government signalling it will act against price inflation, with export curbs and release-quota tightening the standard next steps," he said. High prices, he added, "reliably trigger their own reversal through increased cane planting a season later."

The government has already acted: from September 1, bulk consumers using more than 10 metric tonnes of sugar monthly must limit inventories to 15 days. An earlier order from August 1 capped dealer stocks at 30 days and 4,000 quintals. Sugar exports remain banned until at least September 30, 2026.

"Fundamentals justify strength; they do not justify extrapolation."

— Harshal Dasani, Business Head, INVasset PMS

What to Watch Next

Rahul Sharma of Equity99 named Balrampur Chini Mills as a top pick, citing its 10-factory network with 77,500 TCD crushing capacity and 560 KLD distillery capacity. But across the sector, the next phase of the trade will likely be driven by three catalysts: the annual ethanol procurement price announcement, further downgrades to season production estimates, and whether global prices extend beyond their 14-month high.

The risks are equally clear. Government intervention on prices, a strong cane-planting response setting up next season's surplus, an ethanol-price disappointment, or simple positioning exhaustion after a record month could all trigger a pullback. "The discipline in sugar never changes: it is a trade with a calendar, not a compounding story," Dasani said, "and the ethanol-heavy names are the only ones that blur that line."
